topics.title: Understanding Social Engineering
topics.hook: A text arrives: "Your bank account is locked. Verify within 15 minutes or it will be closed." The link looks almost right. What makes this an attack, and how would you know?
concept: Social engineering attacks people instead of machines. The adversary manipulates trust, fear, or helpfulness so the victim hands over credentials, money, or access on their own.

Attackers lean on a small set of psychological levers: urgency (act now), intimidation (or else), authority (I'm IT / your boss / the bank), and elicitation (casual questions that pull out details piece by piece). The defense is to recognize indicators: mismatched sender addresses, pressure to skip normal steps, requests for secrets, and links whose real destination differs from the text.

Indicators of compromise (IoCs) are the evidence an attack happened or is underway, such as an unexpected password-reset email, a login from an unknown location, or a message you never sent appearing in your sent folder.
terms: Social engineering
Manipulating people into breaking normal security practice.
Phishing
A fraudulent message that impersonates a trusted source to steal data or deliver malware.
Urgency
Pressure to act immediately so the victim doesn't stop to verify.
Intimidation
Threats or fear (fines, account closure, discipline) used to force compliance.
Elicitation
Drawing out sensitive information through seemingly harmless conversation.
Indicator of compromise (IoC)
Observable evidence that a system or account has been attacked.

compare.title: Lever vs. what it sounds like
rows: "Failure to pay will result in legal action."
"This is the CEO. Wire the funds now."
"Fun quiz: what was your first pet's name?"

traps: A message with perfect grammar and a real logo can still be phishing. Judge the request and the sender, not the polish.
Hovering over a link shows its true destination. Clicking it to check is not verification.

items.stem: An email says a user's streaming account will be suspended in one hour unless they confirm payment details via a link. Which social engineering lever is MOST directly being used?
items.why: The one-hour deadline is designed to rush the victim past verification. Elicitation is gradual questioning; tailgating is physical.

items.stem: At a conference, a friendly stranger asks an engineer which VPN client her company uses, what the Wi-Fi naming scheme is, and when the IT team is usually offline. This is BEST described as:
items.why: Small, casual questions that collectively reveal sensitive details are elicitation.

items.stem: Which observation is the STRONGEST indicator of compromise for a personal email account?
opts: A newsletter arrives that the user subscribed to last year
Messages the user never wrote appear in the Sent folder
A password-change reminder from the user's own calendar
items.why: Sent messages the owner didn't write show someone else is using the account.

items.stem: A user receives a text claiming to be from their bank asking them to call a number about fraud. What is the BEST response?
opts: Call the number in the text to ask if it's real
Call the number printed on the back of the bank card
Forward the text to friends as a warning
items.why: Verify through a channel you already trust, not one the attacker supplied.

items.stem: Why do attackers so often impersonate executives or IT staff?
opts: Victims are less likely to question requests from perceived authority
items.why: Authority discourages the victim from pushing back or verifying.

items.stem: A link displays the text www.mybank.com, but hovering shows http://mybank.com.secure-login.ru/verify. What does this indicate?
opts: The bank uses a Russian content server
The link is safe because mybank.com appears in it
The real destination is a different domain controlled by someone else
items.why: The registered domain is the part just before the top-level domain: secure-login.ru, not mybank.com.

items.stem: Which control MOST reduces the damage if a user falls for a credential-phishing email?
items.why: With MFA, a stolen password alone is not enough to log in.

items.stem: A school's staff receive an email impersonating the principal asking them to buy gift cards. Which factor MOST increases the likelihood this attack succeeds?
opts: The email arrives during a busy exam week
The school uses a spam filter
Staff were trained last month on gift-card scams
The principal's real address uses MFA
items.why: Busy, distracted targets verify less, raising likelihood. Training and filtering lower it.

topics.title: Suspicious Website Logins
topics.hook: You get an alert: "New sign-in to your account from a device in another country." You're at home on your laptop. What happened, and what do you do in the next five minutes?
concept: Passwords fail in predictable ways. Attackers guess common passwords, try huge lists automatically, or reuse passwords leaked from other sites. A login alert from an unfamiliar device or location is often the first sign one of these worked.

Strong authentication layers defenses: a long unique password per site (a password manager makes this practical), plus multifactor authentication (MFA), where a second factor such as a one-time password (OTP) from an app or a hardware key is required. If an alert looks real, change the password from a trusted device, sign out other sessions, and review account recovery settings.
Fake login pages are a related trap: a site that copies a real login screen but sits on a different domain. Always check the address bar before entering credentials.
terms: Password attack
Any method of discovering or bypassing a password: guessing, brute force, reuse of leaked credentials.
Multifactor authentication (MFA)
Requiring two or more different kinds of proof (something you know, have, or are).
One-time password (OTP)
A code valid for a single login or a short time window.
Password manager
Software that generates and stores unique strong passwords.
Session
A logged-in state after authentication; ending sessions forces re-login.

compare.title: Weak vs. strong habits
rows: Unique password per site via a manager
Password + app OTP or security key
Verify, reset, sign out other sessions

traps: An OTP sent by text is better than no MFA, but app-based codes or security keys are harder to intercept.
If you reset a password but leave old sessions active, the attacker may stay logged in.

items.stem: A user receives a sign-in alert from an unfamiliar city at 3 a.m. while asleep. What is the MOST likely explanation?
opts: The user's credentials were used by someone else
items.why: A login the user didn't make, from an unfamiliar location, indicates compromised credentials.

items.stem: After confirming the alert above is not theirs, which sequence is BEST?
opts: Delete the alert email and move on
Change the password from a trusted device, sign out all sessions, and enable MFA
Create a new account and keep the old one
Post on social media asking if others got the alert
items.why: Reset removes the stolen secret, signing out ends the attacker's session, and MFA blocks a repeat.

items.stem: Which combination provides true multifactor authentication?
opts: Password and a code from an authenticator app
items.why: MFA requires different factor types. Password + question or PIN are both 'something you know'.

items.stem: An attacker obtains a list of email/password pairs leaked from a gaming site and tries them on banking sites. Why does this often work?
opts: Banks share passwords with gaming sites
Many people reuse the same password across sites
Leaked passwords are automatically valid everywhere
items.why: Password reuse lets one breach unlock many accounts.

items.stem: What is the PRIMARY security benefit of a password manager?
opts: It removes the need for any password
It makes unique, long passwords for every site practical
It hides the user's IP address
items.why: Its value is making strong, unique passwords usable at scale.

items.stem: A login page looks identical to a school's portal, but the address bar reads portal-school-login.net. What should the user conclude?
opts: It is a mirror maintained by the school
It is likely a fake login page harvesting credentials
It is safe because the page uses the school logo
items.why: A different domain hosting a copied login form is a credential-harvesting indicator.

items.stem: Which account would have the HIGHEST impact if compromised?
opts: A primary email account used for password resets on other sites
A free trial of a music app
A forum account with no personal data
items.why: Email that receives reset links can be used to take over many other accounts.

items.stem: Why is a hardware security key or authenticator app generally stronger than an SMS one-time code?
opts: SMS can be intercepted or redirected through SIM swapping
items.why: Text messages can be redirected; app codes and keys are bound to the device itself.

topics.title: Best Practices for Public Networks
topics.hook: At a coffee shop you see two networks: "CoffeeHouse_Guest" and "CoffeeHouse Guest Free". One is the shop's. One isn't. How could you tell, and what protects you either way?
concept: Public Wi-Fi is shared, often unencrypted, and anyone can broadcast a network name. An evil twin is a rogue access point that copies or imitates a legitimate network's SSID (its broadcast name) so victims connect to the attacker instead; everything they send can then be watched or altered.

Wireless networks can also be jammed, flooding the radio frequency so legitimate users can't connect, a form of denial of service (DoS). War driving is cruising an area to map wireless networks and find weak ones.

Protections: confirm the exact network name with staff, prefer HTTPS sites, avoid sensitive tasks on public Wi-Fi, turn off auto-join, and use a virtual private network (VPN), which encrypts traffic in a tunnel between your device and the VPN server so the local network can't read it.
terms: SSID
Service set identifier: the broadcast name of a wireless network.
Evil twin
A rogue access point impersonating a legitimate network.
Jamming
Deliberately interfering with radio signals to block wireless communication.
Denial of service (DoS)
An attack that makes a service unavailable to legitimate users.
War driving
Searching for wireless networks from a moving vehicle to find targets.
VPN
An encrypted tunnel that protects traffic from the local network.

compare.title: Threat vs. protection
rows: Verify SSID, disable auto-join, use VPN
Switch to cellular; it's an availability attack

traps: A VPN protects data in transit on the local network. It does not make a phishing site safe or stop malware.
A network with a familiar name is not proof it's legitimate. SSIDs can be copied exactly.

items.stem: An attacker sets up a hotspot named "Airport_Free_WiFi" next to the real airport network. This is an example of:
items.why: Impersonating a legitimate network's name with a rogue AP is an evil twin.

items.stem: Which tool BEST protects a traveler's traffic from being read by others on hotel Wi-Fi?
items.why: A VPN encrypts traffic between the device and the VPN server.

items.stem: Students in a library suddenly cannot connect to any Wi-Fi, though the access points show as powered on. A device nearby is flooding the 2.4 GHz band with noise. Which attack is this?
items.why: Radio interference that blocks access targets availability: jamming is a DoS.

items.stem: A person drives slowly through a neighborhood with a laptop logging every Wi-Fi network and its security type. This is:
items.why: Mapping wireless networks from a vehicle is war driving.

items.stem: Which setting change MOST reduces the risk of a laptop silently connecting to an evil twin?
items.why: Auto-join lets the device connect to any matching SSID without the user deciding.

items.stem: Once a victim connects to an evil twin, what can the attacker MOST directly do?
opts: Read or alter unencrypted traffic passing through the access point
Change the victim's hardware serial number
Access the victim's offline files without any connection
items.why: The attacker controls the path, so unencrypted traffic is visible and modifiable.

items.stem: A user on public Wi-Fi visits a site over HTTPS but has no VPN. Which statement is MOST accurate?
opts: The page contents are encrypted, but others may still see which site was visited
Nothing is protected without a VPN
HTTPS hides the user's device from the network
items.why: HTTPS encrypts content; metadata like the domain can still leak. A VPN hides more.

items.stem: A café owner wants to detect if an evil twin appears near the shop. Which method is MOST useful?
opts: Periodically scanning for networks broadcasting the café's SSID from unknown hardware
items.why: Scanning for duplicate SSIDs from unrecognized access points reveals rogue APs.

topics.title: AI-Based Cybersecurity Attacks
topics.hook: A parent gets a voicemail in their child's voice, panicked, asking for money. The child is at school and fine. How was the voice made, and what family rule would have stopped it?
concept: Generative AI lowers the cost and raises the quality of social engineering. Large language models (LLMs) can write fluent, personalized phishing in any language at scale. Voice cloning and deepfake video can impersonate a specific person from a few seconds of public audio or video.
AI also speeds technical attacks: generating variations of malware, scanning for weaknesses, or automating password guessing. The core attack goals don't change; the volume and believability do.

Defenses shift from spotting typos to verifying identity through a second, trusted channel: a call-back number you already know, a family or team safe word, approval rules for payments, and MFA that doesn't rely on recognizing a voice or face.
terms: Large language model (LLM)
AI that generates human-like text from patterns learned on large datasets.
Deepfake
AI-generated or altered audio, image, or video that imitates a real person.
Voice cloning
Synthesizing speech that sounds like a specific individual.
Out-of-band verification
Confirming a request through a separate, trusted communication channel.
traps: Good grammar and a familiar voice are no longer evidence of legitimacy.
The best control against deepfakes is procedural (verify out-of-band), not trying to spot visual glitches.

items.stem: A finance clerk joins a video call with what appears to be the CFO, who instructs an urgent wire transfer. The CFO was actually traveling and never on the call. Which threat is MOST likely?
items.why: AI-generated video impersonating a real person is a deepfake.

items.stem: Which control BEST defends against AI voice-cloning scams requesting money?
opts: Requiring a call back to a known number or a pre-agreed safe word
items.why: Out-of-band verification doesn't depend on detecting the fake.

items.stem: Why has generative AI made phishing harder to detect for many users?
opts: It removes all links from emails
It produces fluent, tailored messages without the typos users learned to spot
It only targets computers, not people
items.why: Users relied on poor grammar as a tell; LLMs remove it.

items.stem: A company executive posts many conference talks online. How does this affect AI-enabled attack risk?
opts: It lowers risk because the executive is well known
It increases risk because plentiful audio and video make cloning easier
items.why: More public samples make voice and video impersonation more convincing.

items.stem: An attacker uses an LLM to scrape a target's social media and write messages referencing their real coworkers and projects. This BEST increases which aspect of the attack?
items.why: Personal, accurate details make the pretext more credible.

items.stem: A business wants to prevent deepfake-driven payment fraud. Which layered approach is BEST?
opts: Two-person approval for large transfers plus call-back verification
Training staff to detect pixel artifacts only
Allowing transfers by chat for speed
items.why: Procedural checks with more than one person stop a single deceived employee.

items.stem: Which is an AI-enabled attack on a technical system rather than on a person?
opts: Automatically generating many malware variants to evade signature detection
A cloned voice calling a parent
A fake video of an executive
items.why: Malware variant generation targets detection systems; the others target human trust.

items.stem: An employee receives an urgent voice message from their manager asking for a password. Which detail is the STRONGEST red flag regardless of how real the voice sounds?
opts: The request asks for a secret that policy says is never shared
The message is under one minute long
items.why: A request that violates policy is suspicious no matter who seems to be asking.

topics.title: Leveraging AI in Cyber Defense
topics.hook: A security analyst faces 40,000 alerts a day. A human can review a few hundred. How can AI help, and where can it go wrong?
concept: Defenders use AI to handle scale. Machine learning models flag unusual behavior, such as a login pattern that doesn't match a user's history, faster than people can. LLM assistants summarize logs, explain alerts, draft incident reports, and suggest next steps.
AI helps most with triage: ranking which alerts deserve human attention first. It can also filter spam and phishing, analyze suspicious files, and help write detection rules.

Limits matter. Models make mistakes (false positives waste time; false negatives miss attacks), can be fooled by inputs designed to evade them, and LLMs can state wrong things confidently. Sensitive data shouldn't be pasted into tools without approval. Humans stay accountable for decisions.
terms: Triage
Sorting alerts by urgency so the most important get attention first.
Anomaly detection
Flagging behavior that differs from an established normal baseline.
False positive
An alert on activity that is actually harmless.
False negative
A real attack that produces no alert.
Human in the loop
Keeping a person responsible for reviewing and approving AI-driven actions.
traps: AI doesn't remove the need for analysts. It changes their job toward verifying and deciding.
An AI summary of a log is not evidence. The log itself is.

items.stem: A security team receives far more alerts than staff can review. Which AI use is MOST appropriate?
opts: Ranking alerts by likely severity for human review
items.why: AI triage focuses limited human attention on the riskiest alerts.

items.stem: An AI email filter blocks a legitimate message from a new client. This is an example of:
items.why: Flagging something harmless as malicious is a false positive.

items.stem: Why should an analyst verify an LLM's explanation of a suspicious log before acting on it?
opts: LLMs can produce confident but incorrect statements
Verification is only needed for printed logs
items.why: LLM output can be wrong; the underlying evidence must be checked.

items.stem: A model learns each employee's typical login times and locations, then alerts on deviations. This is:
items.why: Comparing behavior to a learned baseline is anomaly detection.

items.stem: An AI detection system is tuned so aggressively that analysts ignore most alerts. What is the MOST serious consequence?
opts: Real attacks may be overlooked due to alert fatigue
items.why: Too many false positives train people to ignore alerts, including true ones.

items.stem: A student wants to paste a company's internal logs, including employee names and IP addresses, into a public chatbot. What is the PRIMARY concern?
opts: Sensitive data may be exposed outside the organization
The chatbot can't read IP addresses
items.why: Confidential data shouldn't leave approved systems.

items.stem: An attacker slightly modifies malware so an AI classifier labels it benign. This tactic is BEST described as:
items.why: Crafting inputs to fool a model is adversarial evasion.

items.stem: Which is the BEST reason to keep a human in the loop when AI recommends blocking a major customer's IP range?
opts: Blocking may disrupt legitimate business, so a person should weigh the impact
items.why: High-impact actions need human judgment about availability and business effects.
